title: Good Article Breakdown: How Lilian Weng Turns 'Thinking' into a Classification Tree
subtitle: Close Reading of the Structure of Lil'Log's 'Why We Think'
markdown: > Breakdown Target: 'Why We Think', Lilian Weng, Lil'Log, published May 1, 2025, approximately 40 minutes reading time, 53 references, with acknowledgments at the beginning for John Schulman for providing extensive feedback and direct editing. The original link is at the end. This is a structural breakdown in the style of study notes; viewpoints belong to the original author. Test-time compute is the dominant narrative in the current reasoning direction, and this article provides the most complete account of how these ideas developed. The previous article in the 'Good Article Breakdown' section dissected her Agents review; this one, appearing nearly two years later, allows for a comparison of the same author's two organizational methods. ## I. Why It's Worth Dissecting 'Let the model think for a while' spans five fields: psychology, decoding strategies, RL training, architecture design, and scaling laws, with hundreds of references. The organizational solution here is to first build a classification tree, then hang all the literature on its branches: where thinking occurs (token space / continuous space / latent variables) forms the first level of branching, and each branch is further subdivided by mechanism. At any time, the reader knows their position on the tree. Comparison of the architectural axis with the Agents review: that article was divided by system components (Planning / Memory / Tool use), while this one is divided by where computation occurs. The same author's two choices of 'knife' demonstrate the principle of selecting an axis for a review: the axis must be determined by the essential contradiction of the topic. The essential contradiction of agents is component collaboration, while the essential contradiction of thinking is explicit versus implicit computation. ## II. Main Body Skeleton: Three Motivations Take Root, Four Branches Unfold | Chapter | Responsibility | Breakdown Key Points | | --- | --- | --- | | Motivation | Rooting | Three motivations: psychological analogy, computation as a resource, latent variable modeling | | Thinking in Tokens | Branch One | Parallel sampling and sequential correction, RL training for reasoning, tool use, faithfulness | | Thinking in Continuous Space | Branch Two | Recurrent architectures, thinking tokens | | Thinking as Latent Variables | Branch Three | EM algorithm, iterative learning | | Scaling Laws for Thinking Time | Branch 4 | Trade-offs with Pre-training Compute | | What's for Future | Convergence | Six Open Questions | | Citation | Citation Engineering | Provide BibTeX directly at the end, consistent with the Agents survey style | The opening technique of the Motivation section is worth extracting on its own: She first presents a multiplication problem that even humans cannot answer immediately, introducing the idea that 'thinking before answering' is a behavior shared by both humans and models. She then uses Kahneman's dual-process theory to establish the distinction between the fast and slow systems of System 1 and System 2. This progresses through three layers—personal experience, psychological theory, and engineering issues—with each layer taking only a few sentences. ## III. Explicit vs. Implicit: The Duality Structure Running Through the Text The first branch of the classification tree, Thinking in Tokens, discusses explicit thinking: reasoning is made explicit as natural language tokens, readable and monitorable. CoT monitoring can even enable weak models to supervise strong ones. However, faithfulness is questionable. The three failure modes listed by Lanham et al. (premature answering, uninformative tokens, and human-unreadable encodings) indicate that improvements in accuracy do not necessarily depend on human-readable reasoning; directly applying optimization pressure to CoT can also lead to confounding reward hacking, where the model hides its true intentions within the CoT. The second and third branches discuss implicit thinking: cyclic architectures iterate in latent space, where thinking tokens are purely placeholders inserted to purchase additional forward computation. Quiet-STaR generates a rationale after each token and then mixes the prediction. The contrast between explicit and implicit thinking supports the structural tension of the entire text: explicit thinking trades off for interpretability, while implicit thinking trades off for computational efficiency. Faithfulness is the Achilles' heel of the explicit lineage. This duality directly echoes the content of the RL training section: the four-stage process of DeepSeek-R1 and the emergence of the 'Aha moment' are representative works of explicit thinking training, while the failed attempts with PRM and MCTS are also addressed in this section. My continuous tracking of the GRPO to DAPO spectrum finds its upstream narrative in this article. ## IV. Sense of Position in the Scaling Laws Section Branch 4 positions thinking time as a new extension dimension following model scale, training compute, and data volume, but immediately adds boundary conditions: test-time compute and pre-training compute are not one-to-one interchangeable; reasoning tokens must be significantly fewer than pre-training tokens to offer an advantage, and powerful base models remain indispensable. The rigor of the survey lies in marking the applicable boundaries for each hot concept. This section serves as the anchor of the entire text, placed just before the conclusion, which is perfectly timed. ## V. Six Open Questions: An Honest Conclusion to the Survey The "What's for Future" section at the end lists six questions, each representing a genuine unsolved problem in the current landscape: How to incentivize models to generate human-readable and faithful reasoning paths while avoiding reward hacking; How to define and capture reward hacking without human intervention; How to train self-correction when there is no ground truth; How to perform RL with CoT rollout for tasks that are difficult to evaluate, such as creative writing and tutoring; How to distill performance gains back into the base model during deployment; How to make test-time overhead adaptive to problem difficulty. These six questions almost all point to the intersection of alignment and evaluation, mirroring the three challenges outlined at the end of last year's Agents survey. By first establishing opportunities and then delineating boundaries, an honest survey deserves to be cited. ## VI. Three Writing Techniques Worth Learning 1. **The axis is determined by the essential contradiction of the topic**: When choosing an organizational axis for a survey, first ask what the essential tension of this field is. For thinking, the tension is between explicit and implicit; for agents, the tension is between component collaboration. 2. **Dualistic structure supports the skeleton**: The main contrast of the article (explicit vs. implicit) is foreshadowed in the introduction and echoed in each branch, allowing readers to carry the same question throughout the entire text. 3. **Boundary conditions serve as the anchor**: In a survey on hot concepts like test-time compute, a dedicated section is reserved for discussing what it cannot achieve, preventing premature hype. ## Footnote: Mapping to My Own Work The core work of OKC-SFT is reducing hallucination rates (from 34.4% to 15.6%), which essentially addresses the critical vulnerability of explicit thinking in this article: the gap between what the model says and its actual computation. The division of labor in the coaching system—where the "algorithm layer outputs structured JSON evidence" and the "LLM layer performs only semantic paraphrasing"—can be understood as externalizing trusted computation to the algorithm layer, ensuring that even if the LLM layer's paraphrasing contains hallucinations, it cannot fabricate evidence out of thin air. Explicitly verifiable computation is superior to free-form narrative; this principle runs through both this article and my engineering practice. ## References - Original Article: Why We Think, Lilian Weng, Lil'Log, 2025-05-01, lilianweng.github.io/posts/2025-05-01-thinking/ - Original Acknowledgments: John Schulman provided feedback and directly edited. - Reference scale: numbered up to 54, missing 28, actual 53 items - Association breakdown: This blog's Lil'Log Agents review breakdown (good article breakdown section, same author's architecture axis organization method comparison)
